lessons.title: Improving Lagos: The Makoko Floating School & Self-Help

before.content_html:
Two Approaches to Improving Lagos

Improving life for the urban poor in a city growing this fast needs more than one strategy. Lagos uses two main approaches. Top-down planning is led by the government and can deliver large schemes such as roads and railways. Self-help schemes are bottom-up — residents and NGOs work together to build, fix and run things themselves. The strongest improvements usually come where the two work side by side.

The Makoko Floating School

In a slum like Makoko, where every spare metre of dry land is built on, a school for local children seemed almost impossible. In 2013 Nigerian architect Kunlé Adeyemi proposed a radical answer: a school that floated on the lagoon itself. The Makoko Floating School was a triangular three-storey wooden building set on 256 empty plastic barrels, with a green roof, solar panels and a rainwater collection system. It cost around £5,000 to build and could host 100 children.

Crucially, it was a project with the Makoko community rather than imposed on it. Local fishermen helped tow it into place, residents helped run it, and the school used materials that had been thrown away — the barrels were salvaged. It became a global symbol of self-help architecture for slum communities.

Key Fact

The Makoko Floating School was designed by Nigerian architect Kunlé Adeyemi in 2013. It used 256 plastic barrels for buoyancy, solar panels for power and rainwater harvesting for water — and was built with the Makoko community.

In 2016 a heavy storm caused the original school to collapse. Critics said it showed self-help architecture had limits; supporters argued the design had always been a prototype. Adeyemi’s firm went on to develop a stronger second-generation version called MFS II, which was exhibited internationally. The lesson is honest: small, low-cost projects can deliver huge symbolic and practical wins, but they need long-term funding and engineering support to last. Self-help is powerful, but it works best alongside well-resourced top-down planning.

Top-Down Transport: BRT and the Lagos Rail

The Lagos State Government has invested heavily in transport to ease the ‘go-slow’. The Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) system opened in 2008 and now runs along several main corridors. BRT buses use lanes separated from general traffic, so they keep moving while cars sit in jams. Fares are low enough for low-income workers, and journey times have been cut by up to half on some routes. The Lagos Rail Mass Transit project — the city’s first mass-transit railway — opened its first line in 2023, designed to move tens of thousands more commuters off the roads each day.

Improving Water and Sanitation

The Lagos Water Corporation has expanded the mains network and partnered with NGOs to install community boreholes in slum districts — tens of thousands of residents now have safer water than they did a decade ago. NGOs such as WaterAid have built communal toilet blocks in slum areas, with female-only sections to improve safety. Public-health teams run free vaccination campaigns and educate parents about oral rehydration to limit cholera outbreaks. None of these are total solutions, but each one improves life for thousands.

Eko Atlantic and Resilience to Flooding

A second top-down scheme is Eko Atlantic City. It is a new district built on land reclaimed from the Atlantic next to Victoria Island. The project includes a 8-kilometre sea wall called the Great Wall of Lagos, designed to protect the city from rising sea levels and the storm surges that already flood low-lying neighbourhoods every rainy season. Eko Atlantic adds high-end housing, offices and public space — but critics argue it serves the wealthy first, with little direct benefit for the slum residents who suffer most when the city floods.

Key Fact

Eko Atlantic City is built on land reclaimed from the Atlantic. Its 8 km sea wall, the Great Wall of Lagos, is designed to protect Victoria Island and central Lagos from sea-level rise and storm surges.

Self-Help: Energy and Recycling

Bottom-up energy projects are spreading across slum districts. NGOs such as Solar Sister train local women to sell low-cost solar lanterns; households that once relied on smoky kerosene now have clean light for evening homework. Community recycling co-operatives buy plastic bottles and aluminium cans from street pickers, then sell them on to industrial buyers — cleaning up streets and creating informal incomes at the same time. These schemes do not solve the city’s waste crisis on their own, but they demonstrate something important: when residents are paid to recycle, the streets get cleaner.

Government planners often want quick, dramatic results — a flyover, a new sea wall, a tower block. Residents want practical day-to-day fixes — cleaner water, a safer toilet, a school close to home. The most successful Lagos projects combine both. Eko Atlantic protects central Lagos from flooding, but only the BRT, community boreholes and projects like the Makoko Floating School reach families in places like Makoko itself. Top-down delivers the scale; self-help delivers the relevance.

Why It Matters

Improving the quality of life for the urban poor is the central challenge of every fast-growing megacity. Lagos shows that progress is possible — one community borehole, one BRT lane, one floating school at a time — but also that the scale of the problem demands sustained government investment alongside community-led solutions. The next lesson shifts the lens to a UK city, where the challenges look very different.

before.content_html:
A City Made by Migration

Manchester’s population fell during the late twentieth century as factories closed, but it is now growing fast again — both from national migration within the UK and from international migration from outside it. Migration changes the size of a city, the mix of its people and the kinds of opportunities and challenges it faces. To understand modern Manchester you have to understand who has been moving there, and why.

National Migration into Manchester

Tens of thousands of UK residents move into Greater Manchester each year. The single biggest group is students: the four universities have around 100,000 students between them, with the University of Manchester alone hosting roughly 45,000. Many graduates stay on, attracted by lower house prices than London, growing employers in finance, media and digital, and the city’s cultural scene. Families and professionals also move from the south-east to escape London rents. The 2017 opening of the BBC at MediaCityUK pulled hundreds of broadcasters out of London — a clear example of how government policy can redirect national migration.

Key Fact

Manchester’s four universities host around 100,000 students — the city’s biggest national-migration group. Many graduates stay; families and professionals also move from the south-east for cheaper housing and growing employers in finance, media and tech.

International Migration into Manchester

Manchester has been an international city for centuries. Irish migrants arrived in the nineteenth century to work in the mills; Jewish refugees settled in Cheetham Hill in the late 1800s; Caribbean migrants came in the 1950s and 60s; South Asian families — especially from Pakistan, Bangladesh and India — settled across Rusholme and Longsight from the 1960s. More recent waves include EU migrants after eastern European countries joined the EU in 2004, and refugees and asylum seekers from Syria, Afghanistan and Ukraine. The 2021 census found that around 31.4% of Manchester city residents were born outside the UK — one of the highest shares of any English city outside London.

Geographers describe a city’s character as the mix of cultures, languages, food, religion and history that you can feel walking around. Manchester’s Curry Mile on Wilmslow Road in Rusholme grew out of South Asian migration; Chinatown on Faulkner Street is one of Britain’s oldest. The Caribbean Carnival has been part of Manchester’s summer since 1971. Schools teach over 200 languages between them. None of these features would exist without migration — and they now feed back into the economy by drawing tourists and global talent.

Opportunities Created by Migration

Migration has made Manchester a culturally vibrant city — the cultural mix includes festivals like the Caribbean Carnival, Eid celebrations in Platt Fields and Chinese New Year in Chinatown. Migrant communities have driven entrepreneurship: many of the restaurants, takeaways and small businesses in Rusholme, Cheetham Hill and Longsight were founded by first- or second-generation migrants. Migration also fills key jobs — the NHS in Greater Manchester depends heavily on overseas-trained doctors and nurses, and EU migrants have long staffed the construction, hospitality and food-processing sectors.

Urban Challenges: Deprivation and Inequality

For all its growth and energy, Manchester has some of the most deprived neighbourhoods in England. Urban deprivation is measured by the Index of Multiple Deprivation, and Manchester consistently ranks among the most deprived local authorities in England. Wards such as Harpurhey, Gorton and parts of Ardwick have unemployment, child poverty and ill-health rates well above the national average. Life expectancy varies by years across the city — a man in Manchester city centre lives roughly seven years less on average than a man in the wealthier Greater Manchester suburbs.

Key Fact

Manchester’s most deprived wards include Harpurhey, Gorton and Ardwick. Life expectancy is around seven years lower in central Manchester than in the wealthier suburbs. Inequalities cut across housing, education, health and employment.

Inequalities in Housing, Education and Health

In housing, much of Manchester’s Victorian terraced stock is poor quality — damp, cold and expensive to heat. Council housing waiting lists are long, and rough sleeping is rising in the city centre. In education, GCSE attainment in deprived wards is well below the national average, and progression to university is far lower than in suburbs like Trafford. In health, deprived wards have higher rates of smoking, obesity, diabetes and heart disease — partly because lower incomes mean unhealthier diets and higher chronic stress, partly because GP services are stretched. Employment follows the same pattern: even when jobs are growing, those jobs increasingly need degrees.

When the cotton mills closed in the second half of the twentieth century, Manchester lost tens of thousands of skilled jobs. The replacement economy — finance, media, digital, universities — needs different skills, and the workers laid off in the 1970s and 80s did not always get the chance to retrain. Their children inherited the housing, the schools and the health profile of communities that had been built around the old industries. Geographers call this a cycle of deprivation: low incomes lead to poor housing and poor health, which lead to poor educational outcomes, which lead back to low incomes. Breaking the cycle takes long-term, joined-up investment.

Urban Sprawl and the Rural-Urban Fringe

As Manchester has grown again, the built-up area has spread outwards into the countryside — urban sprawl. New estates have appeared in Trafford, Wigan and Stockport on what used to be farmland, and commuter villages like Hale and Knutsford have grown rapidly as families seek green space within reach of city jobs. This puts pressure on the rural-urban fringe: traffic and air pollution rise, hedgerows and woodland are lost, and longer commutes deepen environmental impacts. The conflict between protecting green belt land and building enough new homes is one of the central planning debates in modern Manchester.

Why It Matters

Migration brings the energy, talent and culture that have remade Manchester — but the same growth has deepened housing pressure and exposed the inequalities that linger from the city’s industrial past. The next lesson looks at how Manchester is responding through urban regeneration, brownfield development and urban greening.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • National migration brings around 100,000 students plus families and professionals into Manchester; international migration has shaped the city for centuries, with around 33% of central residents born outside the UK at the 2021 census.
  • Migration has created opportunities — cultural mix in Chinatown and the Curry Mile, NHS staffing, vibrant entrepreneurship — but Manchester also has some of England’s most deprived wards (Harpurhey, Gorton, Ardwick).
  • Inequalities persist in housing, education, health and employment, with a roughly seven-year life-expectancy gap. Urban sprawl into the rural-urban fringe is reshaping commuter villages around Manchester.

lessons.title: Urban Greening, Brownfield Sites & Quality of Life

before.content_html:
Healing the Industrial Wound

When Manchester’s mills, docks and warehouses closed in the second half of the twentieth century, they left behind acres of empty, polluted land. Old factory floors, contaminated soil, derelict canal-side wharves — the kind of land geographers call brownfield sites. The challenge was to turn this dereliction into something useful again. The answer has been a generation of urban regeneration projects, alongside urban greening initiatives that put nature back into the city.

Why Salford Quays Needed Regeneration

The clearest example in Greater Manchester is Salford Quays — once the inland end of the Manchester Ship Canal and one of the busiest ports in Britain. When containerised shipping moved to deeper-water ports in the 1970s, the docks closed almost overnight. By 1985 they had lost around 3,000 jobs, the basins were filled with debris and the surrounding warehouses were derelict. Air and water pollution made the area a no-go zone. Salford Council bought the land and began a long-term regeneration plan that has run for over thirty years.

The Salford Quays Regeneration Project

The project aimed to do four things: clean up the contamination, build new homes, attract employers and create public space. Today Salford Quays includes MediaCityUK (BBC, ITV and around 250 creative-industry firms), the Lowry Theatre and Arts Centre, the Imperial War Museum North designed by Daniel Libeskind, the Old Trafford football and cricket grounds nearby, around 5,000 new homes and the Lowry Outlet shopping centre. The Quays themselves — once polluted basins — now host watersports including dragon-boat racing and an open-water swimming centre. From a derelict dockyard, Salford Quays has become a destination that attracts millions of visitors a year.

Key Fact

Salford Quays is a brownfield regeneration on the closed Manchester Ship Canal docks. The project includes MediaCityUK, the Lowry Centre, the Imperial War Museum North and around 5,000 new homes — transforming a derelict port into a leisure and creative-industries hub.

Planners argue endlessly about whether to build on brownfield sites (already-used land in cities) or greenfield sites (previously undeveloped land). Brownfield protects the countryside, reuses existing roads and rail, and revives areas that would otherwise stay derelict. But it is expensive: contaminated soil must be cleaned, old foundations broken up, and homes built more compactly. Greenfield is cheaper but consumes farmland, raises commuting and weakens green belt protection. UK government policy now requires planning authorities to prioritise brownfield first — one of the reasons projects like Salford Quays have been politically as well as economically attractive.

Urban Greening: Putting Nature Back

Cities are warmer, drier and noisier than the countryside, and they trap air pollution. Urban greening projects aim to soften these problems by adding vegetation back into the built-up area. Sackville Gardens and Mayfield Park — the latter Manchester’s first new city-centre park for over a century, opened in 2022 on a former railway depot — show what urban greening can do. Mayfield Park reclaimed 6.5 acres of brownfield land beside the River Medlock, removed culverts to restore the river, and planted around 140 trees. Green roofs on new buildings (including parts of MediaCityUK), pocket parks in dense neighbourhoods, and tree-planting schemes along main roads all play their part.

Why Greening Matters for Quality of Life

Green space is not just nice to look at. Research summarised by the UK government’s Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs shows it lowers urban temperatures by several degrees in summer, traps fine particulate air pollution, slows heavy rainfall before it reaches drains (reducing flood risk), and supports biodiversity such as bees, butterflies and urban birdlife. For residents, regular access to parks is linked to lower stress, better mental health and higher physical activity. In a city where deprived wards have shorter life expectancies, easy access to green space is a public health intervention as well as an environmental one.

Key Fact

Urban greening cools cities, traps fine air pollution, reduces flood risk and supports residents’ mental and physical health. Manchester’s Mayfield Park (opened 2022, 6.5 acres on former rail land) is the first new city-centre park for over a century.

Sustainable Urban Living: The Bigger Picture

Brownfield regeneration and urban greening sit inside a broader idea: sustainable urban living. The principles include energy and water conservation in homes, recycling waste rather than sending it to landfill, creating green space for residents, and designing transport so people can move without private cars. Manchester has expanded its Metrolink tram network — now Britain’s largest light rail system — with low fares aimed at cutting car use. The new Bee Network integrates buses, trams, bikes and walking under one ticketing system. These transport strategies aim to cut traffic congestion, lower air pollution and make city living possible without owning a car.

Cars produce nitrogen dioxide and fine particulates that harm respiratory health, especially in deprived inner-city wards close to busy roads. Manchester’s Metrolink expansion (which now runs over 90 stops including the Trafford Park and Airport lines) and the city’s growing cycle network reduce the number of car journeys. Lower traffic volume means lower emissions, lower noise, safer streets and more space for trees, pavement cafés and pocket parks. Greening, transport and brownfield regeneration are best understood as one strategy — making the city work better for the people who live in it.

Why It Matters

From the Salford docks to the railway depot at Mayfield, Manchester shows how brownfield regeneration and urban greening can take the worst legacy of an industrial city and turn it into a strength. The same lessons apply to every UK city wrestling with the long shadow of deindustrialisation: build on what is already used, plant trees, design transport so cars are not the default, and quality of life rises across the board.

before.content_html:
What Does ‘Sustainable’ Mean in a City?

Sustainable urban living is about running a city so it works for the people in it today and still works for their grandchildren. UK cities use about three-quarters of the country’s energy and produce most of its waste, so getting urban life right matters for the whole planet. Sustainable cities cut pollution, manage resources carefully and let people move around without choking the air.

Key Fact

The four main features of sustainable urban living are: water conservation, energy conservation, waste recycling and creating green space. All four reduce a city’s ecological footprint.

Water Conservation

UK households use roughly 140 litres of water per person each day. Sustainable cities cut that figure in three ways. Homes are fitted with water meters so families pay for what they use — meters typically cut consumption by around 15%. Low-flush toilets, aerated taps and dual-flush systems lower demand inside the home. Outside, rainwater is harvested from roofs into water butts to water gardens, and grey water from showers is recycled to flush toilets in newer developments.

Energy Conservation

Heating and lighting buildings is the biggest single use of energy in UK cities. Sustainable building reduces this through thick insulation, double or triple glazing, LED lighting and smart meters that show householders what they are spending. New flagship districts such as BedZED in south-east London were designed from the start to be carbon-neutral, combining solar panels with super-insulated homes. Across the wider city, solar panels on rooftops and small-scale wind turbines feed renewable electricity into the grid.

UK cities now recycle just under half of household waste. Kerbside collections separate paper, glass, metals, plastics and food waste so they can be reprocessed instead of buried in landfill. Food waste can be sent to anaerobic digesters, which produce biogas to generate electricity. Bristol’s ‘closed-loop’ scheme turns food waste from city schools into compost used on city allotments — the same nutrients re-enter the local food system.

Creating Green Space

Parks, street trees and roof gardens cool a city by 2–4°C in summer, soak up rainwater to cut flood risk, and absorb carbon dioxide and air pollution. They also boost mental health: studies by the University of Exeter found that people living within sight of green space report lower stress. London’s ‘National Park City’ status, declared in 2019, set a target of making 50% of the capital green by 2050 through new pocket parks, green roofs and tree planting.

Key Fact

Urban green space cools the city, reduces surface flooding, absorbs CO₂ and improves mental health. London aims to become a 50% green city by 2050.

Why Traffic Congestion Matters

Traffic congestion wastes time, fuel and money — the consultancy INRIX estimated that the average London driver lost roughly 156 hours stuck in jams in 2022. It also causes serious air-quality problems: emissions of nitrogen dioxide and particulates from petrol and diesel engines are linked to thousands of early deaths in UK cities each year. Sustainable transport strategies aim to shift people out of single-occupancy cars and onto cleaner alternatives.

An integrated transport system joins buses, trains, trams and cycle hire under one ticket, like Manchester’s Bee Network. Park-and-ride sites at the edge of the city let drivers leave cars and ride a frequent shuttle bus into the centre. Congestion charging — London charges £15 a day to enter the central zone — pushes drivers onto public transport. Pedestrianised streets, cycle highways and Low Traffic Neighbourhoods reclaim space for walkers and cyclists.

London’s Ultra-Low Emission Zone (ULEZ) charges £12.50 a day for older, more polluting vehicles. Within two years of expansion, roadside nitrogen-dioxide levels in inner London fell by around 40%. Electric buses and trams produce no roadside pollution at all.

Putting It Together: Curitiba and Freiburg

Two cities are often used as global models. Curitiba in Brazil pioneered the bus rapid-transit system — long ‘bendy’ buses run in dedicated lanes with raised stations, so 70% of commuters use public transport. Freiburg in Germany combines a dense tram network, car-free residential districts (Vauban) and powerful incentives for solar power; over 25% of the city’s electricity comes from renewables. Both show that joining transport, energy and green space planning together creates a measurably more sustainable city.

lessons.title: Measuring Development: GNI, HDI & the DTM

before.content_html:
Why Measure Development?

Development is uneven across the planet — some countries are very rich, with long lives and good schools, while others struggle with poverty and disease. Geographers measure development so that aid can be targeted, governments can compare progress, and patterns of inequality become visible. The challenge is that no single number captures everything that matters about a country’s quality of life.

Key Fact

Development is measured using two types of indicator: economic measures (GNI per head, employment) and social measures (life expectancy, literacy, infant mortality). HDI combines both into one score from 0 to 1.

Economic Indicators

The most common economic measure is Gross National Income (GNI) per head. It adds up everything a country’s citizens and businesses earn, including overseas income, and divides by population. Norway’s GNI per head is around US$95,000; Burundi’s is around US$240. The gap is enormous. Economists also track unemployment rates and the share of workers in primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary industries — richer countries tend to have far more service-sector jobs.

Social Indicators

Social indicators measure quality of life. Infant mortality is one of the most sensitive: in the UK around 4 babies in 1,000 die before their first birthday, while in Sierra Leone the figure is over 80. Life expectancy ranges from 84 years in Japan to under 55 in some sub-Saharan African countries. Literacy rates measure education access, and the number of people per doctor shows healthcare provision — the UK has roughly 3 doctors per 1,000 people; Malawi has fewer than 0.05. Access to safe water completes the picture: where less than 60% of people have clean water, child deaths from diarrhoea soar.

Every single indicator has weaknesses. GNI per head is an average — it hides huge inequality. A country can have an oil-rich elite and a poor majority, yet still record high GNI. Data may be old, missing or unreliable, especially in poorer countries. Some economic activity goes unrecorded in the informal economy — an estimated 70% of African workers earn this way. Social indicators have their own issues: literacy may be self-reported, and life expectancy averages mask whether men or women, rich or poor, live longer.

The Human Development Index

To overcome the weaknesses of single measures, the United Nations created the Human Development Index (HDI). It blends three dimensions: a long, healthy life (life expectancy), knowledge (mean and expected years of schooling) and a decent standard of living (GNI per head). Each country gets a score between 0 and 1. Norway and Switzerland sit above 0.95, the UK around 0.93, India around 0.64, and Niger near 0.40. HDI is more useful than GNI alone because it shows whether wealth is being turned into education and health.

Key Fact

HDI combines life expectancy, education (years of schooling) and GNI per head. Scores run from 0 to 1: UK around 0.93, India around 0.64, Niger around 0.40.

The Demographic Transition Model

The Demographic Transition Model (DTM) links population change to development. As a country develops, both birth and death rates fall, but at different times. The gap between them shapes population growth.

Stage 1 — High fluctuating: birth and death rates both high, population stable. Now found only in remote tribal communities.

Stage 2 — Early expanding: death rate falls due to better food, water and medicine, but birth rate stays high. Population grows fast. Examples: Afghanistan, parts of sub-Saharan Africa.

Stage 3 — Late expanding: birth rate falls as women gain education, contraception spreads and child labour becomes less needed. Population still grows but more slowly. Examples: India, Brazil.

Stage 4 — Low fluctuating: both rates low, population steady. Examples: UK, USA, Australia.

Stage 5 — Decline: birth rate falls below death rate, so population shrinks and ages. Examples: Japan, Germany, Italy.

Linking the DTM to Development

The DTM lines up neatly with the development indicators. Stage 2 countries usually have low GNI, high infant mortality and HDI below 0.55. Stage 3 countries are the classic NEEs — rapid growth, falling birth rates, HDI rising past 0.65. Stage 4 countries are HICs with high GNI and HDI above 0.85. Stage 5 introduces a new problem: an ageing population means fewer workers supporting many pensioners. The DTM is not perfect — it was based on European history and assumes every country follows the same path — but it is a powerful way of linking population change to development.

A World That Is Not Flat

Wealth and quality of life are not spread evenly. The richest 10% of the global population owns more than half of all wealth, while billions live on under US$2.15 a day — the World Bank’s 2022 extreme poverty line. Uneven development is the result of physical, economic and historical forces working together over decades and centuries, and it has powerful consequences for the people caught on the wrong side of the gap.

Key Fact

The three main groups of causes of uneven development are physical (climate, location, hazards), economic (trade and debt) and historical (colonialism, conflict). The main consequences are wealth and health gaps and large-scale migration.

Physical Causes

Geography matters. Landlocked countries such as Chad, Mali and Burkina Faso lack ports, so importing and exporting goods is expensive and slow. A harsh climate — whether the heat and aridity of the Sahel or the seasonal rains of Bangladesh — makes farming risky and disease, like malaria, more common. Tropical regions lose roughly 1% of GDP a year to malaria alone. Frequent natural hazards compound the problem: Haiti has been hit by earthquakes, hurricanes and cholera outbreaks, each of which destroys infrastructure faster than it can be rebuilt. Poor soils, deserts and mountains all add to the difficulty.

Economic Causes

Many low-income countries depend on exporting primary commodities — cocoa, coffee, cotton, copper, oil. World market prices for these goods swing wildly: cocoa farmers receive about 6–10% of the price of a chocolate bar, while the chocolate company keeps most of the rest. Trade rules favour rich countries: they pay low tariffs on raw beans, but high tariffs on processed chocolate, locking poorer countries into low-value exports. Heavy national debt — some HIPCs have spent more on interest payments than on schools and hospitals combined — further drains money out of poorer economies.

From the 16th century, European powers conquered much of Africa, Asia and the Americas. Under colonialism, raw materials were extracted to feed European factories while local industries were suppressed. Borders were drawn by colonial powers without regard for ethnic groups — in much of Africa this still fuels tension today. After independence, many countries inherited weak institutions, single-crop economies and external debt. Civil wars in places such as the Democratic Republic of Congo and Sierra Leone destroyed decades of progress.

Consequences: Wealth and Health

The first consequence of uneven development is dramatic gaps in wealth and health. The average UK citizen lives 26 years longer than a citizen of Sierra Leone. A baby born in Norway has roughly 20 times the lifetime income of a baby born in Burundi. Malnutrition still affects around 750 million people worldwide. Within countries, the gap can be just as wide: in Brazil, the richest 10% earn 38% of national income, leaving the poorest with very little. These disparities are not just numbers — they shape every part of daily life.

Consequences: International Migration

When the gap is large enough, people move. International migration is driven by a mix of push and pull factors. Push factors include unemployment, low wages, conflict, drought and poor public services. Pull factors include higher incomes, safer cities, better schools and hospitals, and family already living abroad. In 2022 the UN estimated that 281 million people lived outside their country of birth. Mexico to USA, North Africa to southern Europe, Syria to Germany, and South Asia to the Gulf states are some of the world’s biggest migration streams.

Key Fact

Push factors driving migration include conflict, drought, low wages and lack of jobs. Pull factors include safer cities, better wages, better schools and existing family abroad.

Source countries often gain from remittances — in Tajikistan and South Sudan they account for over 30% of GDP. But they also lose skilled workers in a phenomenon called ‘brain drain’ — the Philippines trains nurses who then move to the UK or USA. Host countries gain a younger, working-age population that pays taxes, but face pressure on housing, schools and political tensions over identity.

Why It Matters

Uneven development is not just a moral concern — it shapes the global economy, drives mass migration and sustains conflict. Closing the gap means tackling all three causes together: investment in physical infrastructure, fairer trade rules to share the benefits of globalisation, and political stability after a long history of colonialism. The next lesson looks at the strategies designed to do exactly that.

lessons.title: Closing the Gap: Aid, Trade & Tourism in The Gambia

before.content_html:
Strategies to Close the Gap

Reducing the development gap means lifting incomes, life expectancy and education in poorer countries faster than they rise in richer ones. Geographers identify seven main strategies: investment, industrial development, tourism, aid, intermediate technology, fair trade and microfinance loans, plus debt relief. None works in isolation; the best results come from combining them.

Key Fact

The seven main strategies for reducing the global development gap are: investment, industrial development, tourism, international aid, intermediate technology, fair trade, and microfinance loans / debt relief.

Investment, Industry and Aid

Foreign direct investment by transnational corporations builds factories that bring jobs and skills. Industrial development — especially manufacturing — can lift millions out of poverty, as it has in Bangladesh’s textile sector. International aid can be short-term humanitarian relief after a disaster or long-term development funding for schools, clinics and infrastructure. Aid sometimes attracts criticism: it can create dependency or be misused if governments are corrupt, so charities such as Oxfam favour aid that builds local capacity rather than handouts.

Intermediate Technology and Microfinance

Intermediate technology uses simple, affordable, locally repairable tools rather than expensive imported machinery. Examples include hand-drilled wells in Malawi, treadle pumps in Bangladesh and clay pot fridges in Sudan. Microfinance loans — pioneered by the Grameen Bank in Bangladesh — give people small amounts of capital to start businesses such as a sewing workshop or vegetable stall. Repayment rates are over 95%, and women run most of the loans, helping their families and communities together.

Fair trade guarantees farmers a minimum price for crops like coffee, cocoa and bananas, plus a community premium spent on schools or clean water. The Fairtrade Foundation works with around 1.9 million farmers worldwide. Debt relief — for example through the IMF’s Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) initiative — has cancelled over US$100 billion of poor-country debt since 1996, freeing money for schools and healthcare.

Tourism: Why It Works

Tourism is one of the fastest ways to inject money into a poorer country’s economy. It creates jobs in hotels, restaurants, transport and crafts, and earns valuable foreign currency. The multiplier effect means that money spent by tourists is re-spent locally on food, building materials and education. Tourism also drives investment in airports, roads and electricity that benefit everyone.

Case Study: Tourism in The Gambia

The Gambia is the smallest country on the African mainland, with a population of around 2.6 million and a GNI per head of just under US$800. It has used tourism since the 1960s as a development strategy, attracting around 600,000 visitors a year before the pandemic, mostly from the UK, Netherlands and Belgium escaping the European winter for sandy Atlantic beaches and the warm dry season from November to April.

Tourism contributes roughly 20% of The Gambia’s GDP and provides around 42,000 direct jobs — one in six adults. Hotels at Kotu, Kololi and Senegambia employ chefs, drivers, guides, cleaners and gardeners. The Gambia Tourism Board’s ‘Roots’ festival celebrates the country’s links with the African diaspora, attracting visitors from the USA. Foreign currency earned by tourism pays for medicines and equipment that the government could not otherwise afford.

Local craft markets and the ‘Tourism Concern’ initiative make sure money reaches small businesses, not only big resorts. New schools and clinics have been built using a tourism levy. Improved infrastructure — the upgraded Banjul airport and a coastal road — benefits Gambians as well as tourists.

Costs and Limits of Tourism

Tourism is not perfect. Around 60% of money spent at all-inclusive resorts can leak straight back to overseas tour operators, an effect known as economic leakage. Most tourism jobs are seasonal and low-paid, and many close completely in the wet summer months. Tourism is fragile: visitor numbers in The Gambia collapsed during COVID-19 and during periods of political unrest. There can be cultural and environmental costs too, from pressure on freshwater to local resentment of wealthier visitors.

Key Fact

Tourism brings around 20% of GDP and one in six adult jobs in The Gambia. Limits include economic leakage of up to 60% to overseas firms, seasonal work, and vulnerability to crises like COVID-19.

Bringing the Strategies Together

No single strategy closes the development gap by itself. The Gambia uses tourism alongside fair trade groundnut exports, microfinance loans for women’s cooperatives, and aid from the UK, EU and World Bank. The clearest progress comes when investment in jobs, fairer trade rules and aid for health and education are pursued together — and when local communities, not only foreign companies, share in the gains.

before.content_html:
Why Study Nigeria?

Nigeria is the obvious case study for an emerging economy. It is Africa’s most populous country (around 225 million people in 2024 and rising fast), Africa’s largest economy by GDP for most of the last decade, and one of the world’s top ten oil producers. Yet around 40% of Nigerians still live below the national poverty line. It is a textbook example of a Newly Emerging Economy (NEE) — growing fast, but with deep inequalities still to address.

Key Fact

Nigeria has around 225 million people, the largest economy in Africa, but ~40% of the population lives below the poverty line. Oil and gas account for roughly 7% of GDP but over 80% of export earnings.

Location and Regional Importance

Nigeria sits in West Africa, on the Gulf of Guinea coast. It borders Benin to the west, Niger to the north, Chad to the north-east and Cameroon to the east. The Atlantic coastline gives it major ports at Lagos and Port Harcourt, opening trade with Europe, the Americas and increasingly Asia. The country lies entirely within the tropics, between roughly 4°N and 14°N, so it has a hot climate but a sharp north-south rainfall divide. Nigeria is a founder member of ECOWAS, the African Union, OPEC and the Commonwealth, giving it diplomatic weight far beyond its borders.

Global Importance

Globally, Nigeria matters for three reasons. First, oil: it is the largest oil producer in Africa and a major supplier to Europe and the USA. Second, culture: Nigerian Afrobeats music (Burna Boy, Wizkid, Tems) and Nollywood films are exported across the world — Nollywood produces around 2,500 films a year, second only to India in volume. Third, demographics: Nigeria is projected to overtake the USA as the world’s third most populous country before 2050. Where Nigeria goes, Africa often follows.

Nigeria gained independence from Britain in 1960. It was ruled by a sequence of military governments from the 1960s through the 1990s, with a brutal civil war (the Biafran War, 1967–70) early on. Stable democratic elections have been held every four years since 1999, and peaceful handovers of power between parties (notably 2015 and 2023) have boosted investor confidence. Corruption remains a serious challenge: Nigeria scored 25/100 in the Transparency International Corruption Perceptions Index in 2023, ranking among the bottom third globally.

Social and Cultural Context

Nigeria is one of the most diverse countries in the world, with over 250 ethnic groups and 500 languages. Three groups dominate: the Hausa-Fulani in the north, the Yoruba in the south-west and the Igbo in the south-east. The country is roughly 53% Muslim (mostly in the north) and 45% Christian (mostly in the south). This diversity is a source of vibrant culture but also of tension — the Islamist Boko Haram insurgency in the north-east has displaced over two million people since 2009. The 2014 kidnapping of 276 Chibok schoolgirls drew global condemnation.

Key Fact

Nigeria has over 250 ethnic groups, dominated by the Hausa-Fulani (north), Yoruba (south-west) and Igbo (south-east). The country is roughly 53% Muslim (north) and 45% Christian (south).

Environmental Context

Nigeria’s landscape varies dramatically from north to south. The far north is part of the Sahel, with under 500 mm of rain a year and creeping desertification. The Middle Belt has wooded savanna grassland used for cattle grazing and grain crops. The south-east holds the remains of West African tropical rainforest, while the Niger Delta is a vast wetland of mangroves, creeks and oil pipelines. Climate change is making the north drier and the rainfall in the south heavier and less predictable, hitting farmers hardest.

Nigeria’s mix of features shapes its development. Oil reserves in the Niger Delta have made the country wealthy on paper, but pollution from spills and gas flaring has damaged fisheries and farmland for local communities. Coastal Lagos is one of Africa’s biggest ports and home to Africa’s largest stock exchange, but it is also the world’s fastest-growing megacity. Northern droughts and southern flooding both push migration to the cities, fuelling the urbanisation studied in earlier lessons.

Why Nigeria Is an NEE

Nigeria ticks every box of an emerging economy. GDP grew at an average of 5–7% a year between 2000 and 2014, lifting tens of millions out of extreme poverty. The economy has diversified beyond oil into telecoms, banking and Nollywood. A young population (median age just 18) provides a growing workforce. Yet challenges remain: 40% poverty, regional inequality (the south is much richer than the north), corruption and Boko Haram. Understanding the political, social and environmental setting is the first step to understanding everything else about Nigeria’s development — and the next two lessons build on it.

An Islamist insurgent group that has carried out attacks in north-east Nigeria since 2009, including the 2014 kidnapping of 276 schoolgirls in Chibok.
A semi-arid belt of grassland and acacia trees stretching across northern Africa, prone to drought and the spread of the Sahara.

lessons.title: Nigeria: Aid, Environmental Cost & Quality of Life

before.content_html:
The Other Side of NEE Growth

The previous lesson focused on the engines of Nigeria’s growth — manufacturing, TNCs and trade. This lesson looks at the consequences. Aid has helped fund schools, healthcare and disaster recovery. But rapid economic development has come with a heavy environmental price tag, and the benefits have not reached every Nigerian equally. Quality of life has improved on average yet inequality remains stark.

Key Fact

Nigeria receives short-term and long-term aid, top-down (large infrastructure) and bottom-up (community-led) projects. Major donors include the UK, USA, the World Bank and Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

Types of Aid Nigeria Receives

There are four main categories of aid. Short-term emergency aid follows disasters — the UN sent food and clean water after the 2022 Nigeria floods, which killed over 600 people and displaced 1.4 million. Long-term development aid funds infrastructure, health and education over many years; the UK’s former Department for International Development (DFID, now part of FCDO) has spent hundreds of millions of pounds on Nigerian schools and clinics. Top-down aid is large-scale projects organised by governments or international bodies — for example, the World Bank’s funding for the Lagos urban water network. Bottom-up aid is small, community-led projects organised by NGOs such as ActionAid Nigeria, which trains village women in farming techniques.

Positive impacts: Aid funds clinics that have helped cut under-5 mortality from over 200 per 1,000 in 1990 to around 110 today. Polio was officially eliminated in Nigeria in 2020 thanks to a combined World Health Organization, UNICEF and Gates Foundation vaccination drive. NGOs help women set up small businesses, raising rural incomes.

Negative impacts: Aid can be misused if government corruption diverts money from intended recipients — Transparency International has flagged this risk repeatedly. Aid can create dependency rather than self-reliance. Some critics argue donors attach conditions that benefit them, like requiring spending on companies from the donor country.

Environmental Impacts of Development

Nigeria’s rapid growth has caused serious environmental damage. The Niger Delta is the worst-affected area: oil spills from rusting pipelines have leaked over 13 million barrels of crude into the creeks and mangroves since the 1970s — equivalent to roughly 50 Exxon Valdez disasters. Spills kill fish and crops on which 60% of Delta residents rely for food. Gas flaring — burning off waste gas from oil wells — releases massive amounts of CO₂ and toxic particulates; Nigeria is one of the world’s biggest gas flarers despite official bans.

Beyond the Delta

In the north, growing populations and Sahel droughts are causing desertification — about 350,000 hectares of land turn to desert every year. In Lagos, fast urban growth has filled lagoons with waste, raised air pollution to dangerous levels and put pressure on freshwater. Industrial output has tripled since 2000, but environmental regulation has not kept pace, with factories often discharging untreated effluent into rivers. Climate change is a force multiplier: heavier rainstorms in the south worsen flooding while the north becomes drier.

Key Fact

Three big environmental costs: oil spills and gas flaring in the Niger Delta, desertification in the north (350,000 hectares lost a year) and air and water pollution in fast-growing cities like Lagos.

Effects on Quality of Life

For many Nigerians, life is genuinely improving. Average life expectancy has climbed from 47 in 1990 to around 55 today. Access to safe water has risen above 70% in cities. Mobile phone ownership is over 90%, opening up banking and education. School enrolment is rising. The economy has lifted tens of millions out of extreme poverty. Yet quality of life remains uneven.

Around 40% of Nigerians still live below the national poverty line. Inequality is sharp between regions: Lagos State has a poverty rate around 4%; Sokoto State in the north sees rates over 80%. Rural communities lack reliable power, with daily blackouts even in cities. The Niger Delta’s oil-bearing communities suffer poorly compensated pollution while wealth flows to Abuja and abroad. Boko Haram’s violence has destroyed schools and clinics in the north-east. Quality of life depends sharply on where in Nigeria you are born.

Putting It Together

Nigeria’s case study brings together everything in this unit on changing economic worlds. Manufacturing, TNCs and new trade links have lifted millions out of poverty and boosted Africa’s position globally. Aid has helped tackle disease and disaster. But the environmental price — oil pollution, desertification, urban smog — falls hardest on the poor, and the wealth created has not yet reached every region. The work of development is unfinished.

lessons.title: Post-Industrial UK: Science Parks & Rural Change

before.content_html:
After the Factories: A Service Economy

As traditional industries shrank, the UK economy did not collapse — it changed shape. The country became a post-industrial economy, where most jobs are in services and high-tech research rather than mining, smelting or shipbuilding. Three areas have grown especially fast: information technology, service industries and finance, and research clustered around science and business parks. Together they have created millions of new jobs — though they are not always located where the old jobs disappeared.

Key Fact

The UK’s post-industrial economy is built on three pillars: information and communication technology (ICT), financial and business services, and research clustered in science and business parks. Together they account for the majority of UK economic output today.

Information Technology

The ICT industry covers software design, mobile networks, cloud computing, gaming and digital media. The UK has more than 1.7 million ICT jobs and the sector contributes over £150 billion a year to the economy. Major hubs include the M4 corridor west of London (often called ‘Silicon Roundabout’s sibling’), Cambridge and Manchester. ICT is attractive because it requires only modest physical infrastructure compared with heavy industry — offices, fast broadband and skilled workers, rather than coal supplies and railway lines.

Service Industries and Finance

Banking, insurance, retail, healthcare, education and tourism dominate UK employment. London is one of the world’s top financial centres alongside New York and Tokyo — the City and Canary Wharf alone employ over half a million people in finance. The growth of universities has turned cities like Oxford, Edinburgh and Manchester into major exporters of higher education. The NHS is one of the world’s largest employers with over 1.4 million staff.

Science Parks and Business Parks

A science park is a planned cluster of research-led firms, often attached to a university. The Cambridge Science Park, founded by Trinity College in 1970, now hosts over 130 companies in biotechnology, pharmaceuticals and software. Co-locating businesses lets staff share ideas, recruits and equipment — what economists call ‘agglomeration’. Business parks are similar but for tertiary firms (offices, headquarters), usually on city outskirts with good motorway access.

Modern industry can be more environmentally sustainable than the factories of the 1970s. Nissan’s plant in Sunderland is the UK’s largest car factory and produces electric Leaf and Qashqai vehicles. The site is partly powered by an on-site wind farm of ten turbines, captures rainwater for use in production, and reuses solvent from paint shops. Newer manufacturing demonstrates that industry and environmental responsibility can coexist — an idea now spreading to steelworks (electric arc furnaces) and chemical plants (carbon capture).

Rural Areas of Population Growth

Economic change reshapes the countryside as well as the cities. Some rural areas are gaining population through counter-urbanisation. South Cambridgeshire is a good example. Its population has grown by over 20% since 2001 because:

  • Commuter access: the area is within 30 minutes of Cambridge and around an hour of London by train, so professionals can live rural while working in the city.
  • Quality of life: villages offer cheaper houses than central Cambridge, good schools, less traffic and more open space.
  • Remote work: faster broadband and the rise of home-working since 2020 mean fewer journeys are required at all.

The downsides include rising house prices that price out younger locals, traffic on small village roads and pressure on services such as doctors’ surgeries.

Rural Areas of Population Decline

Other rural areas are losing people. The Outer Hebrides off the north-west coast of Scotland have seen population fall by over 50% since 1900 — though the recent decline has slowed. Causes include:

  • Lack of jobs: the local economy depends on fishing, crofting (small-scale farming) and tourism — all seasonal or low-paid.
  • Out-migration of young people: teenagers leave for university and rarely return, leaving an ageing population.
  • Declining services: as population falls, schools, post offices and bus routes close, making the area less attractive still.

Local authorities in declining rural areas use several strategies. The Outer Hebrides council has invested in faster broadband to attract remote workers, supported small craft and food businesses through grants, and worked with the Scottish government to subsidise ferry routes that keep the islands connected. Affordable housing schemes try to keep young families on the islands rather than losing them to the mainland. Progress is slow, but population decline has flattened compared with earlier decades.

Key Fact

South Cambridgeshire (growth, near Cambridge) and the Outer Hebrides (decline, remote north-west Scotland) show how access to jobs, services and city links determines whether a rural area gains or loses people. Rural change is not one trend — it depends on location.

Why This Matters

The shift to a post-industrial economy is uneven. Some places — Cambridge, the M4 corridor, central London — have flourished. Others — remote uplands, former mining towns, isolated coastal communities — have not. The next lesson asks why this divide between north and south, and between thriving and struggling regions, is one of the biggest challenges facing the UK economy.

lessons.title: The North-South Divide & the UK in the Wider World

before.content_html:
A Country of Two Halves?

If you draw a line from the Severn Estuary to the Wash, you separate the UK into a richer south-east and a poorer north and west. Geographers call this the north–south divide. The pattern is not absolute — there are wealthy towns in the north (Harrogate, Cheshire) and pockets of poverty in the south (parts of east London, Plymouth) — but on most measures the gap is real.

Key Fact

Wages in London are around 30% higher than the UK average, while parts of the north-east sit roughly 15% below it. Life expectancy in Glasgow is around 73 for men, compared with 82 in parts of West Sussex — a gap of nine years.

Why the Divide Exists

The divide grew partly out of the previous lesson’s story. Deindustrialisation hit the north, the Midlands, south Wales and central Scotland hardest, because that is where coal, steel and shipbuilding were concentrated. The new growth sectors — finance, ICT, biotech — are clustered in London, Cambridge, Oxford and the M4 corridor. London also benefits from being the political and financial capital, attracting head offices, embassies and the highest-paid jobs. Connectivity makes it worse: a train from London to Brighton takes an hour, but Manchester to Leeds (less than half the distance) can take just as long.

The north–south description is a useful shortcut but hides smaller divides. Some London boroughs (Tower Hamlets, Newham) have child poverty rates above 40%, similar to deprived parts of Liverpool or Middlesbrough. Equally, the ‘Golden Triangle’ of Cambridge, Oxford and London is even richer than the rest of the south. The divide is partly a regional one, partly a city-versus-coalfield one, and partly a global-economy-versus-old-economy one.

Strategies to Resolve the Divide

UK governments have tried for decades to rebalance the economy. Some of the main strategies:

  • Northern Powerhouse: a strategy launched in 2014 to link Manchester, Leeds, Liverpool, Sheffield and Newcastle into a single ‘mega-city region’ with shared transport, science investment and devolved powers.
  • Devolution deals: giving city-region mayors (Greater Manchester, West Yorkshire, Liverpool City Region) control over local transport, housing and skills budgets.
  • Enterprise zones: areas with tax breaks for new businesses, designed to attract investment to former industrial sites such as Tees Valley.
  • Levelling Up Fund: a multi-billion-pound programme of grants for transport, regeneration and cultural projects in towns that have fallen behind.

Transport Investment

Transport projects are central to closing the divide because better connectivity attracts business. Major examples include:

  • Rail upgrades: the Elizabeth Line (Crossrail) opened in 2022 to speed up east–west journeys across London. The Trans-Pennine Route Upgrade is electrifying the Manchester–Leeds–York line. HS2 Phase 1 will eventually link London and Birmingham, though northern sections have been scaled back.
  • Roads: the A14 Cambridge to Huntingdon improvement (opened 2020) eased a major freight bottleneck. Smart-motorway upgrades have added capacity on parts of the M1, M6 and M62.
  • Airports and ports: Heathrow handles around 80 million passengers a year. Manchester is the third-busiest UK airport. Felixstowe handles roughly 40% of UK container traffic, linking the country to Asian and European supply chains.

The UK in the Wider World

The UK is one of the most connected countries on Earth. Its position straddling the Atlantic and Europe, English-speaking workforce and historic global links shape its economy and culture.

  • Trade: the UK exports around £700 billion of goods and services a year. The European Union remains its largest trading partner; the United States is the largest single-country market. Other big partners include China, Japan and India.
  • Culture: UK music, film, TV (BBC, Netflix UK productions) and football (the Premier League) are watched worldwide. The English language itself is a major export, with overseas students learning it bringing £30 billion+ a year into UK universities and language schools.
  • Transport links: Heathrow, the Channel Tunnel and the Port of Felixstowe make the UK a global gateway. Submarine cables across the Atlantic carry the majority of internet traffic between Europe and North America.
  • Political links: through the Commonwealth, the United Nations, NATO and trading agreements with the European Union, the UK shapes and is shaped by global decisions.
Key Fact

The UK’s global links run through trade (EU and US lead), culture (Premier League, BBC, English language teaching), transport (Heathrow, Felixstowe, the Channel Tunnel) and politics (Commonwealth, NATO, UN).

Even after leaving the European Union in 2020, the UK still does roughly half its trade with EU member states. Geography matters — the EU is the closest large market — and supply chains built up over forty years cannot easily be redirected. The Trade and Cooperation Agreement signed at the end of 2020 keeps tariff-free trade for most goods, though customs checks and paperwork have added cost and delay.

Why This Matters

Understanding the divide and the UK’s global links matters because both shape opportunities for ordinary people. A child born in Glasgow has different prospects from one born in Surrey, and a UK exporter relies on Heathrow, the Channel Tunnel and the Port of Felixstowe to reach customers. Closing the divide while staying globally competitive is the central challenge of UK economic policy — and a topic the next two lessons return to from the resource side.

lessons.title: Resource Management: Food, Water & Energy in the UK

before.content_html:
Why Resources Matter

Food, water and energy are the three resources every country needs to keep working. Without enough of any one of them, businesses close, hospitals struggle and people go hungry. Geographers call the way societies plan, share and protect these essentials resource management. The UK has plentiful supplies of fresh water and a developed economy that can buy what it does not grow, but its supply systems are changing fast as imports rise, water demand shifts and the energy mix moves away from fossil fuels.

Key Fact

The UK now imports nearly half its food, transfers water from the wet north and west to the dry south-east, and has shifted its electricity generation from over 70% coal in 1990 to over 40% renewables today.

Food in the UK

In 1984 the UK produced around 78% of the food it consumed. Today that figure is closer to 60% — meaning over 40% is imported. Demand has changed: shoppers expect strawberries in December and avocados year-round. Add modern lifestyles that prefer ready meals, and the result is rising food miles — the distance food travels from farm to plate.

Year-round demand for ‘summer’ produce means UK supermarkets fly green beans from Kenya, mangetout from Peru and tomatoes from Spain. Each step adds to the carbon footprint, so movements such as ‘Buy British’, farmers’ markets and farm shops have grown in response. Many supermarkets now label produce with country-of-origin and carbon scores, and some chefs have built menus around seasonal British vegetables to push back against airfreighted imports.

Two further trends shape UK food supply:

  • Agribusiness: the rise of large-scale, highly mechanised farms producing cereals and dairy efficiently — but with concerns over biodiversity loss, fertiliser run-off and animal welfare.
  • Local sourcing: a movement toward shorter supply chains that supports rural economies and lowers food miles, though prices are usually higher.

Water in the UK

The UK has plenty of water overall — but it is not in the right places. Over half of UK rainfall falls on the north and west, while two-thirds of the population lives in the drier south and east. Areas of water deficit include London, the East Midlands and East Anglia, where less than 700 mm of rain falls a year. Areas of water surplus include western Scotland, the Lake District and Wales, with over 2,000 mm a year.

To match supply to demand, the UK relies on water transfer schemes. The Kielder Water reservoir in Northumberland (the largest in the UK) sends water south through the Tyne, while the Elan Valley in mid-Wales has supplied Birmingham since 1904. Demand keeps rising as population grows and people use more water at home (washing machines, dishwashers, gardens). Quality is also a challenge — agricultural run-off, sewage discharges and microplastics put pressure on water companies to clean water before it reaches taps and rivers.

Energy in the UK

The UK’s energy mix has changed dramatically. In 1990 coal generated over 70% of UK electricity; in 2024 less than 1%. The last coal-fired power station, Ratcliffe-on-Soar, closed in late 2024. Today the mix is roughly:

  • Renewables (over 40%): wind (especially North Sea offshore farms like Hornsea), solar, hydro and biomass.
  • Natural gas (around 30–35%): still the largest single source, used in ‘peaking’ power stations that fill gaps when wind drops.
  • Nuclear (around 12–15%): from stations such as Sizewell B and Hinkley Point B (the last reactor closed in 2022); Hinkley Point C is under construction.
  • Imports and other: via interconnectors with France, Norway and the Netherlands.
Key Fact

UK domestic supplies of coal, gas and oil are all in decline. North Sea oil and gas peaked around 1999 and now produces less than half its peak volume, leaving the UK increasingly reliant on imports and renewable generation.

Economic and Environmental Trade-offs

Every energy choice has both economic and environmental costs. Fossil-fuel extraction creates jobs and tax revenue but warms the climate; nuclear is low-carbon but produces radioactive waste and is expensive to build; wind farms are clean but face local opposition over views, bird strikes and turbine noise. Some areas with surviving North Sea oil and gas (Aberdeen) depend heavily on the industry for skilled jobs, while areas with new offshore wind (Hull, Grimsby) are emerging as a green industrial cluster. Resource policy is rarely just about engineering — it is also about employment, regional balance and climate commitments.

In 2019 the UK was the first major economy to commit by law to reach net-zero greenhouse-gas emissions by 2050. That target shapes resource policy across food (lower-carbon farming), water (energy used for treatment) and energy (rapid expansion of wind and solar). Interim targets include reaching net-zero electricity by around 2035. The pace of change here is faster than almost any other country — though the cost and the impact on workers in fossil-fuel industries remain contested.

Why This Matters

A high-income country can be food, water and energy insecure too. The UK’s rising food imports, growing water transfers and shifting energy mix all show how the modern resource challenge is no longer just about scarcity — it is about sustainability, climate change and security of supply. The next two lessons zoom out to the global picture and then close with one community renewable scheme that shows what sustainable energy can look like at small scale.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • UK food self-sufficiency has fallen from around 78% in 1984 to about 60% today, raising food miles and pushing back movements like local sourcing and seasonal eating.
  • UK water demand is concentrated in the dry south-east while supply is in the wet north and west, so transfers from Kielder Water and Elan Valley are essential.
  • The UK’s energy mix has shifted from over 70% coal in 1990 to over 40% renewables today, though imports and natural gas remain important and nuclear capacity is being rebuilt at Hinkley Point C.

Examiners reward specific places, dates and figures over vague claims.

Secure: identifies the surplus and deficit regions with one named example each. Developing: vague claim about 'rich countries having more food'. Emerging: states there is an unequal distribution without describing the pattern.

practice_questions.text: Explain how conflict can lead to food insecurity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — conflict prevents farmers planting and harvesting, destroys irrigation and storage infrastructure, displaces people from agricultural land, cuts transport routes so food cannot reach markets, and diverts government spending from agriculture to military. Named example: Yemen, South Sudan or Syria. Secure: one clear mechanism with example. Developing: states conflict 'makes farming harder' without mechanism. Emerging: vague link between conflict and food.

practice_questions.text: Suggest how food insecurity can cause social and environmental problems.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three developed points covering both social and environmental — social: price spikes hit poorest households (over 50% of income on food in many African countries); food riots and political instability (Arab Spring 2010–11); chronic undernutrition stunts children's development (149 million children under five). Environmental: over-farming depletes soil (24 billion tonnes of topsoil lost per year); deforestation to open new farmland; over-grazing degrading pasture. Secure: two clear points with evidence, covering at least one social and one environmental. Developing: lists problems without development. Emerging: one vague point.

practice_questions.text: Assess the extent to which climate is the most important factor affecting food supply.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument acknowledging the power of climate (drought, flooding, extreme heat reducing yields, climate change increasing frequency of extreme events) but weighing it against other factors — conflict (famine in Yemen and South Sudan caused by war, not climate), poverty (farmers lack seeds, tools and credit even in fertile areas), technology (HIC yields 5–10 times higher per hectare than LIC), water stress (70% of global freshwater used in farming), pests and disease (East Africa locust crisis 2020–21 affected 23 million). Reaches a justified judgement (e.g. 'climate sets broad boundaries but poverty and conflict turn a poor harvest into a famine'). Secure: two-sided argument with two factors compared. Developing: lists factors with limited evaluation. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without comparison.

lessons.title: Global Water Insecurity: Surplus, Deficit & Impacts

before.content_html:
Water: The Resource You Cannot Live Without

Of all Earth's water, only around 3% is fresh, and two thirds of that is locked in glaciers and ice caps. The tiny remainder — less than 1% of all water — fills rivers, lakes and aquifers on which humanity depends. Yet that 1% is unevenly distributed, and as global demand rises, the mismatch between where water is and where people need it is growing into one of the defining crises of the 21st century. Geographers call this water insecurity — a state in which demand either exceeds supply or where pollution and poor infrastructure make water unreliable even where it exists.

Key Fact

Only around 3% of Earth's water is fresh, and less than 1% is accessible in rivers, lakes and shallow aquifers. Around 2 billion people currently live in countries experiencing high water stress, and the UN projects that by 2025 two thirds of the world's population could face water shortages.

Global Patterns of Water Surplus and Deficit

Water availability is measured as the volume of freshwater available per person per year, adjusted for seasonal variability. Water surplus regions — tropical Central Africa (Congo basin), equatorial South America (Amazon), much of South-East Asia and Scandinavia — receive heavy, reliable rainfall and have relatively small populations. Water scarcity is most severe in the Middle East and North Africa (Libya, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait), where rainfall averages below 100 mm a year, as well as parts of Central Asia, the Sahel and northern India where demand from rapidly growing populations outstrips supply.

Two main forces push global water demand upward:

  • Rising population: more people drink more, cook more and produce more wastewater. The global population passed 8 billion in 2022 and is growing fastest in already water-scarce regions of Africa and the Middle East.
  • Economic development: as countries industrialise and living standards rise, water use increases sharply. Industry (manufacturing, power generation) and commercial agriculture consume vast volumes. A single litre of bottled water requires several litres in production; a car requires around 400,000 litres to manufacture. Higher incomes also mean longer showers, washing machines and garden irrigation.

Agriculture accounts for roughly 70% of all freshwater withdrawals globally — most of it for irrigation. Industry takes around 20%, used for cooling power stations, processing food and manufacturing. Domestic use (drinking, cooking, sanitation, hygiene) accounts for only about 10%. This balance matters for policy: cutting domestic use has a modest impact; improving the efficiency of irrigated agriculture is the single biggest lever available for reducing global water demand.

Factors Affecting Water Availability

Several factors determine whether a country or region can access enough safe water:

  • Climate: rainfall, evaporation rates and seasonality set the natural water budget. Areas with monsoon climates receive most of their rainfall in a few intense months, creating seasonal extremes of flood and drought. Climate change is intensifying these extremes — wetter wet seasons, drier dry seasons, and shifting monsoon timings — making water planning harder.
  • Geology: permeable rock types such as limestone and chalk store water in underground layers called aquifers, which can supply water even in dry seasons. Impermeable basement rocks (much of sub-Saharan Africa) hold little groundwater, so surface rainfall is all that is available — and that is seasonal and unreliable.
  • Pollution of supply: industrial discharge, agricultural run-off (fertilisers and pesticides), untreated sewage and mining waste contaminate rivers, lakes and groundwater. In Bangladesh, naturally occurring arsenic in shallow tubewells poisoned millions of people who drilled for clean water. In China, rapid industrialisation has severely polluted many major rivers.
  • Over-abstraction: pumping groundwater faster than it recharges permanently lowers aquifer levels. In northern India the water table beneath the Punjab farmland is falling by around 1 metre a year as tube wells extract water for irrigation. Saudi Arabia has largely depleted its 'fossil' aquifers — ancient water that accumulated over thousands of years and will not refill in any human timescale.
  • Limited infrastructure: even where water exists, it cannot be used without treatment plants, pipe networks and pumping stations. Around 2.2 billion people lack access to safely managed drinking water, mostly because governments lack the money to build and maintain the necessary infrastructure — not because water is physically absent.
  • Poverty: poor households often pay more for water (from water trucks or vendors) than rich households do on tap, because they cannot afford the connection fees or live beyond the pipe network. In countries without municipal supply, collecting water from rivers or ponds takes hours each day, a burden that falls disproportionately on women and girls.

Impacts of Water Insecurity

When water supply is unreliable or inadequate, the consequences affect health, food, economy and politics:

  • Waterborne disease and water pollution: when people drink from contaminated sources, diseases such as cholera, typhoid, dysentery and diarrhoea spread rapidly. Diarrhoeal disease kills around 1.5 million people a year globally, including around 495,000 children under the age of nine, mostly in LICs. In 2010, an earthquake in Haiti damaged water infrastructure, triggering a cholera outbreak that killed nearly 10,000 people.
  • Reduced food production: agriculture needs reliable water to function. As aquifers fall and rivers run low, irrigated farmland goes out of production. In California's Central Valley, a decade of drought forced farmers to fallow millions of acres and draw down groundwater reserves. Across the Sahel, reduced river flow has shrunk irrigable land, pushing millions toward food insecurity.
  • Industrial output: factories, power stations and mines need water for cooling, processing and transport. In India during a 2019 water crisis, several cities reported that industries were shutting down because municipal water supply had failed. Thermal power stations, which need water for cooling, cut output when rivers run low during droughts.
  • Potential for conflict: where rivers cross national boundaries, upstream users who divert or dam water reduce supply for downstream countries. The Nile is shared by 11 countries; Ethiopia's Grand Renaissance Dam (completed in 2020) triggered a prolonged diplomatic and strategic crisis with Egypt and Sudan, who depend on the Nile for over 90% of their fresh water. The UN has identified over 150 potential future water conflict zones globally.
Key Fact

Water insecurity causes waterborne disease (diarrhoeal disease kills around 1.5 million people a year, including around 495,000 children), reduces food production (drought fallowing in California's Central Valley), cuts industrial output and power generation, and drives geopolitical conflict — most starkly over the Nile, shared by 11 countries.

Egypt receives virtually no rainfall and depends on the Nile for about 97% of its fresh water. Ethiopia, upstream, began filling the reservoir behind its Grand Renaissance Dam in 2020. Egypt and Sudan argued this would cut Nile flow during filling, damaging their agriculture. Ethiopia, one of Africa's poorest and most populous nations, argued it had the right to develop its own hydroelectric resource. No final legal agreement has been reached, illustrating how water scarcity can turn resource development in one country into an existential threat for another.

Why This Matters

Water insecurity is not an abstract environmental issue — it kills people, destroys harvests, closes factories and starts conflicts. As climate change alters rainfall patterns and as population and development drive demand ever higher, the gap between supply and need will widen in many parts of the world. The next lesson explores the strategies — from massive transfer projects to simple rainwater harvesting — that can close that gap sustainably.

glossary_terms.definition: A situation in which demand for fresh water exceeds reliable supply, or where quality is so poor that supply is effectively reduced.
A country or region where water availability per person per year falls below 1,700 cubic metres, making water shortage a periodic or permanent constraint on development.
An underground layer of permeable rock or sediment that holds water and allows it to flow, serving as a source for wells and springs.
